topics.title: Adding fractions with the same denominator

questions.stem: Find the sum: \(\dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{5}{9}\)
questions.hint: When adding fractions with the same denominator, just add the numerators.
questions.solution: Since the denominators are the same, add the numerators: \\\\(2 + 5 = 7\\). The denominator stays \\\\(9\\). The sum is \\(\frac{7}{9}\\).

steps.explain: Check if the denominators are the same.
Add the numerators and keep the denominator.

questions.stem: Calculate \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) + \(\dfrac{2}{5}\).
questions.hint: Same denominator: add the numerators and keep the denominator; then simplify.

steps.explain: The fractions have the SAME denominator 5, so we are adding 5ths: the size of each piece stays the same and we just count pieces.

steps.explain: Simplify \(\dfrac{4}{4}\): the highest common factor of 4 and 4 is 4, so divide the top and the bottom by 4.
\(\dfrac{4}{4}\) divides exactly: \(4 \div  4 = 1\).
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

questions.hint: Same denominator: add the numerators and keep the denominator; then simplify.

steps.explain: The fractions have the SAME denominator 8, so we are adding 8ths: the size of each piece stays the same and we just count pieces.

steps.explain: \(\dfrac{13}{8}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(13 \div  8 = 1\) remainder 5.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: Equal gaps between marks; count the parts from 0.

steps.explain: Simplify \(\dfrac{15}{10}\): the highest common factor of 15 and 10 is 5, so divide the top and the bottom by 5.
\(\dfrac{3}{2}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(3 \div  2 = 1\) remainder 1.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: Equal gaps between marks; count the parts from 0.

questions.stem: Draw a number line to calculate this addition. \(\dfrac{4}{11}\) + \(\dfrac{6}{11}\)

steps.explain: The fractions have the SAME denominator 11, so we are adding 11ths: the size of each piece stays the same and we just count pieces.

questions.stem: Draw a number line to calculate this addition. \(\dfrac{27}{100}\) + \(\dfrac{63}{100}\)
questions.hint: Same denominator: add the numerators and keep the denominator; then simplify.

steps.explain: The fractions have the SAME denominator 100, so we are adding 100ths: the size of each piece stays the same and we just count pieces.
Add the numerators and keep the denominator 100: \(27 + 63 = 90\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{90}{100}\): the highest common factor of 90 and 100 is 10, so divide the top and the bottom by 10.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: Equal gaps between marks; count the parts from 0.

questions.hint: A fraction is more than 1 when the numerator is bigger than the denominator (8).

steps.explain: 'More than 1 loaf' means the fraction is bigger than 1 whole. A fraction with the denominator 8 is bigger than 1 when the numerator is bigger than 8 (because 8/\(8 = 1\)).
Sat: \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) → numerator 3 is 8 or less, so not more than 1 loaf.
Sun: \(\dfrac{2}{8}\) → numerator 2 is 8 or less, so not more than 1 loaf.
Mon: \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) → numerator 7 is 8 or less, so not more than 1 loaf.
Tue: \(\dfrac{9}{8}\) → numerator 9 is bigger than 8, so more than 1 loaf.
Wed: \(\dfrac{11}{8}\) → numerator 11 is bigger than 8, so more than 1 loaf.
Thu: \(\dfrac{10}{8}\) → numerator 10 is bigger than 8, so more than 1 loaf.
Fri: \(\dfrac{4}{8}\) → numerator 4 is 8 or less, so not more than 1 loaf.
The days with more than 1 loaf are Tuesday (\(\dfrac{9}{8}\)), Wednesday (\(\dfrac{11}{8}\)) and Thursday (\(\dfrac{10}{8}\)).
Why the other answers are wrong: they leave out one of the days or include a day with 8 or fewer eighths (Monday is \(\dfrac{7}{8}\), less than a whole loaf).

questions.stem: Find the sum: \(2\dfrac{1}{3} + 1\dfrac{1}{4}\)
questions.hint: Add the whole numbers together, then add the fractions by finding a common denominator.
questions.solution: First, add the whole numbers: \\\\(2 + 1 = 3\\). Next, add the fractions: \\(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4}\\). The common denominator is \\\\(12\\). \\(\frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{12}\\) and \\(\frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{12}\\). Add them: \\(\frac{4}{12} + \frac{3}{12} = \frac{7}{12}\\). Combine with the whole number: \\\\(3\frac{7}{12}\\).

steps.explain: Add the whole number parts.
Find a common denominator for the fractional parts (\(3\) and \(4\)).
Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with denominator 12.
Add the fractions and combine with the whole number.

questions.hint: Since 4 is a multiple of 2, rewrite \(\dfrac12\) with a denominator of 4.

Add the numerators now that the denominators match.

questions.stem: Use shaded parts of rectangles to add \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) and \(\dfrac{3}{10}\).
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (5, 10), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 5, 10.
List multiples: multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15 ; multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30. The lowest common multiple is 10.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) to 10ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 2 (because \(5 \times  2 = 10\)).

questions.stem: Use oranges cut into halves, quarters and eighths to help you calculate this addition. \(1\dfrac{1}{2}\) + \(2\dfrac{1}{8}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: There are mixed numbers. Add the whole numbers first, then deal with the fractions.
Whole numbers: \(1 + 2 = 3\).
The denominators are different (2, 8), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 2, 8.
List multiples: multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. The lowest common multiple is 8.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to 8ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 4 (because \(2 \times  4 = 8\)).

questions.stem: Calculate this addition together as a class. \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{6}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (4, 6), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4, 6.
List multiples: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12 ; multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18. The lowest common multiple is 12.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) to 12ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(4 \times  3 = 12\)).

questions.stem: Calculate this addition together as a class. \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) + \(\dfrac{2}{3}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (2, 3), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 2, 3.
List multiples: multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6 ; multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9. The lowest common multiple is 6.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to 6ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(2 \times  3 = 6\)).

steps.explain: There are mixed numbers. Add the whole numbers first, then deal with the fractions.
Whole numbers: \(2 + 1 = 3\).
The denominators are different (3, 2), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 2, 3.
List multiples: multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6 ; multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9. The lowest common multiple is 6.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) to 6ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 2 (because \(3 \times  2 = 6\)).

questions.stem: Add these fractions. \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{8}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (4, 8), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4, 8.
List multiples: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. The lowest common multiple is 8.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) to 8ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 2 (because \(4 \times  2 = 8\)).

questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

List multiples: multiples of 50: 50, 100, 150 ; multiples of 100: 100, 200, 300. The lowest common multiple is 100.

Change \(\dfrac{2}{50}\) to 100ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 2 (because \(50 \times  2 = 100\)).

Simplify \(\dfrac{5}{100}\): the highest common factor of 5 and 100 is 5, so divide the top and the bottom by 5.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 24. Add the numerators: \(9 + 22 = 31\).
\(\dfrac{31}{24}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(31 \div  24 = 1\) remainder 7.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 20. Add the numerators: \(14 + 16 = 30\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{30}{20}\): the highest common factor of 30 and 20 is 10, so divide the top and the bottom by 10.
\(\dfrac{3}{2}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(3 \div  2 = 1\) remainder 1.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) + \(\dfrac{2}{12}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{6}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (4, 12, 6), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4, 6, 12.
List multiples: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12 ; multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18 ; multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. The lowest common multiple is 12.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) to 12ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(4 \times  3 = 12\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 20. Add the numerators: \(8 + 2 + 11 + 4 = 25\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{25}{20}\): the highest common factor of 25 and 20 is 5, so divide the top and the bottom by 5.
\(\dfrac{5}{4}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(5 \div  4 = 1\) remainder 1.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 7: Fraction arithmetic

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{2}{7}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{14}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{7}\) + \(\dfrac{5}{14}\) + \(\dfrac{3}{7}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (7, 14, 7, 14, 7), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 7, 14.
List multiples: multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21 ; multiples of 14: 14, 28, 42. The lowest common multiple is 14.
Change \(\dfrac{2}{7}\) to 14ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 2 (because \(7 \times  2 = 14\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 14. Add the numerators: \(4 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 6 = 18\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{18}{14}\): the highest common factor of 18 and 14 is 2, so divide the top and the bottom by 2.
\(\dfrac{9}{7}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(9 \div  7 = 1\) remainder 2.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 7: Fraction arithmetic

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{5}{16}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{8}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{16}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (16, 8, 4, 16), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4, 8, 16.
List multiples: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 ; multiples of 16: 16, 32, 48. The lowest common multiple is 16.
Change \(\dfrac{5}{16}\) to 16ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 1 (because \(16 \times  1 = 16\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 16. Add the numerators: \(5 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 12\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{12}{16}\): the highest common factor of 12 and 16 is 4, so divide the top and the bottom by 4.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{8}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{16}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (2, 4, 8, 16), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 2, 4, 8, 16.
List multiples: multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 ; multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 ; multiples of 16: 16, 32, 48. The lowest common multiple is 16.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to 16ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 8 (because \(2 \times  8 = 16\)).

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) + \(\dfrac{8}{20}\) + \(\dfrac{4}{30}\) + \(\dfrac{7}{15}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (3, 20, 30, 15), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 3, 15, 20, 30.
List multiples: multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 ; multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60 ; multiples of 20: 20, 40, 60 ; multiples of 30: 30, 60, 90. The lowest common multiple is 60.
Change \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) to 60ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 20 (because \(3 \times  20 = 60\)).
Change \(\dfrac{8}{20}\) to 60ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(20 \times  3 = 60\)).
Change \(\dfrac{4}{30}\) to 60ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 2 (because \(30 \times  2 = 60\)).
Change \(\dfrac{7}{15}\) to 60ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 4 (because \(15 \times  4 = 60\)).
Now every fraction has denominator 60. Add the numerators: \(40 + 24 + 8 + 28 = 100\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{100}{60}\): the highest common factor of 100 and 60 is 20, so divide the top and the bottom by 20.
\(\dfrac{5}{3}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(5 \div  3 = 1\) remainder 2.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

questions.hint: Find a common denominator before subtracting.
questions.solution: The lowest common denominator for \\\\(8\\) and \\\\(4\\) is \\\\(8\\). Convert \\(\frac{1}{4}\\) to \\(\frac{2}{8}\\). Now subtract: \\(\frac{7}{8} - \frac{2}{8} = \frac{5}{8}\\).

questions.stem: Find the difference: \(4\dfrac{1}{5} - 1\dfrac{1}{2}\)
questions.hint: Convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions, then find a common denominator.
questions.solution: Convert to improper fractions: \\\\(4\frac{1}{5} = \frac{21}{5}\\) and \\\\(1\frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}\\). Common denominator is \\\\(10\\). \\(\frac{21}{5} = \frac{42}{10}\\) and \\(\frac{3}{2} = \frac{15}{10}\\). Subtract: \\(\frac{42}{10} - \frac{15}{10} = \frac{27}{10}\\). Convert back to a mixed number: \\\\(2\frac{7}{10}\\).

questions.stem: Work out this subtraction. Draw a rectangle to show your working. \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) − \(\dfrac{1}{8}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are different (4 and 8). Change both fractions to a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4 and 8 is 8.
Change \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) to 8ths: multiply top and bottom by 2.

questions.stem: Work out this subtraction. Draw a rectangle to show your working. \(\dfrac{9}{10}\) − \(\dfrac{1}{5}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are different (10 and 5). Change both fractions to a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 10 and 5 is 10.
Change \(\dfrac{9}{10}\) to 10ths: multiply top and bottom by 1. (It already has this denominator.)

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{7}{10}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (10): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{5}{10}\).
7 is more than 5, so \(\dfrac{7}{10}\) is more than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between ½ and 1.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

steps.explain: Simplify \(\dfrac{2}{12}\): the highest common factor of 2 and 12 is 2. Divide the top and the bottom by 2.
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{1}{6}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (6): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{3}{6}\).
1 is less than 3, so \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) is less than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between 0 and ½.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

questions.stem: Work out the subtraction, then sort the answer into one of three groups. \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) − \(\dfrac{2}{10}\). Which group is the answer in?
questions.hint: Subtract first. Then compare the answer with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) using the same denominator.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are different (5 and 10). Change both fractions to a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 5 and 10 is 10.
Change \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) to 10ths: multiply top and bottom by 2.

Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{3}{5}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (5): use denominator 10: \(\dfrac{6}{10}\) and \(\dfrac{5}{10}\).
6 is more than 5, so \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) is more than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between ½ and 1.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

steps.explain: Simplify \(\dfrac{2}{12}\): the highest common factor of 2 and 12 is 2. Divide the top and the bottom by 2.
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{1}{6}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (6): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{3}{6}\).
1 is less than 3, so \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) is less than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between 0 and ½.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

questions.stem: Work out the subtraction, then sort the answer into one of three groups. \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) − \(\dfrac{3}{8}\). Which group is the answer in?
questions.hint: Subtract first. Then compare the answer with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) using the same denominator.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are the same (8), so we take away 3 pieces from 7 pieces. Each piece is \(\dfrac{1}{8}\); the crossed-out pieces are taken away.

steps.explain: Simplify \(\dfrac{9}{18}\): the highest common factor of 9 and 18 is 9. Divide the top and the bottom by 9.
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{1}{2}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (2): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
1 is equal to 1, so \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) is equal to \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is equivalent to ½.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

steps.explain: Simplify \(\dfrac{15}{24}\): the highest common factor of 15 and 24 is 3. Divide the top and the bottom by 3.
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{5}{8}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (8): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{4}{8}\).
5 is more than 4, so \(\dfrac{5}{8}\) is more than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between ½ and 1.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

questions.hint: Subtract first. Then compare the answer with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) using the same denominator.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are different (10 and 7). Change both fractions to a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 10 and 7 is 70.
Change \(\dfrac{9}{10}\) to 70ths: multiply top and bottom by 7.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{7}\) to 70ths: multiply top and bottom by 10.
Now subtract the numerators and keep the denominator 70: \(63 - 10 = 53\).
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{53}{70}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (70): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{35}{70}\).
53 is more than 35, so \(\dfrac{53}{70}\) is more than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between ½ and 1.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{2}{15}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (15): use denominator 30: \(\dfrac{4}{30}\) and \(\dfrac{15}{30}\).
4 is less than 15, so \(\dfrac{2}{15}\) is less than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between 0 and ½.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

questions.stem: Work out the subtraction, then sort the answer into one of three groups. \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) − \(\dfrac{3}{12}\). Which group is the answer in?
questions.hint: Subtract first. Then compare the answer with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) using the same denominator.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are different (5 and 12). Change both fractions to a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 5 and 12 is 60.
Change \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) to 60ths: multiply top and bottom by 12.
Change \(\dfrac{3}{12}\) to 60ths: multiply top and bottom by 5.
Now subtract the numerators and keep the denominator 60: \(48 - 15 = 33\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{33}{60}\): the highest common factor of 33 and 60 is 3. Divide the top and the bottom by 3.
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount.
Now sort the answer \(\dfrac{11}{20}\): compare it with \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Change \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) to the same denominator as the answer (20): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) = \(\dfrac{10}{20}\).
11 is more than 10, so \(\dfrac{11}{20}\) is more than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). It is between ½ and 1.
Why the other groups are wrong: the answer is not smaller/equal/larger than \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in those ways.

questions.stem: Mara made a cake and cut it into 8 equal pieces. Her brother ate 1 piece. Mara took the remaining cake to a party, where her friends ate 5 pieces. She took home what was left. What fraction of the whole cake did Mara bring home?
questions.hint: Take away the brother's piece and the friends' pieces from 8 pieces; simplify.

steps.explain: The whole cake is cut into 8 equal pieces, so each piece is \(\dfrac{1}{8}\) of the cake. Mara starts with all 8 pieces.

questions.stem: Matthew is an apprentice electrician. He started the day with \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) of a whole roll of cable. He used \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) of a whole roll in the morning, and \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of a whole roll in the afternoon. How much cable did Matthew have left at the end of the day?
questions.hint: Common denominator first; then take away both amounts.

steps.explain: Take away each amount one after the other (or add the amounts taken and subtract once). First find a common denominator for all the fractions.
The denominators are 8, 3, 4. The lowest common multiple is 24.
Change \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) to 24ths: multiply the top and bottom by 3.

questions.stem: Use the most suitable strategy to subtract these mixed numbers. \(2\dfrac{1}{4}\) − \(\dfrac{3}{4}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
Strategy 2: change both mixed numbers to improper fractions, then subtract. (A mixed number: whole × denominator + numerator, over the denominator.)
\(2\dfrac{1}{4}\) as an improper fraction: \(2 \times  4 + 1 = 9\), over 4.
\(\dfrac{3}{4}\) as an improper fraction: it is already a fraction.
Subtract the numerators: \(9 - 3 = 6\), over 4.
Simplify \(\dfrac{6}{4}\): the highest common factor of 6 and 4 is 2. Divide the top and the bottom by 2.
\(\dfrac{3}{2}\) is an improper fraction (numerator bigger than denominator). Divide: \(3 \div  2 = 1\) remainder 1, so it is 1 and \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount (shown here as decimals).
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the denominators as well (only the numerators are subtracted), one is a piece too big, one a piece too small, and one adds instead of subtracting.

keyPoints.note: A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

questions.stem: Use the most suitable strategy to subtract these mixed numbers. \(2\dfrac{7}{8}\) − \(1\dfrac{3}{4}\)

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
Strategy 1: subtract the whole numbers first, then subtract the fractions.
Whole numbers: \(2 - 1 = 1\).
Fractions: change to the common denominator 8: \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) = \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) and \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) = \(\dfrac{6}{8}\).
Subtract the fractions: \(7 - 6 = 1\), so the fraction part is \(\dfrac{1}{8}\).
Put the whole number part and the fraction part together: 1 and \(\dfrac{1}{8}\).
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount (shown here as decimals).
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the denominators as well (only the numerators are subtracted), one is a piece too big, one a piece too small, and one adds instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: Use the most suitable strategy to subtract these mixed numbers. \(5\dfrac{2}{18}\) − \(4\dfrac{3}{9}\)

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
Strategy 2: change both mixed numbers to improper fractions, then subtract. (A mixed number: whole × denominator + numerator, over the denominator.)
\(5\dfrac{2}{18}\) as an improper fraction: \(5 \times  18 + 2 = 92\), over 18.
\(4\dfrac{3}{9}\) as an improper fraction: \(4 \times  9 + 3 = 39\), over 9.
The denominators are 18 and 9: use the common denominator 18. \(\dfrac{92}{18}\) = \(\dfrac{92}{18}\) and \(\dfrac{39}{9}\) = \(\dfrac{78}{18}\).
Subtract the numerators: \(92 - 78 = 14\), over 18.
Simplify \(\dfrac{14}{18}\): the highest common factor of 14 and 18 is 2. Divide the top and the bottom by 2.
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount (shown here as decimals).
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the denominators as well (only the numerators are subtracted), one is a piece too big, one a piece too small, and one adds instead of subtracting.

keyPoints.note: A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

questions.stem: Use the most suitable strategy to subtract these mixed numbers. \(2\dfrac{5}{6}\) − \(1\dfrac{2}{3}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
Strategy 1: subtract the whole numbers first, then subtract the fractions.
Whole numbers: \(2 - 1 = 1\).
Fractions: change to the common denominator 6: \(\dfrac{5}{6}\) = \(\dfrac{5}{6}\) and \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) = \(\dfrac{4}{6}\).
Subtract the fractions: \(5 - 4 = 1\), so the fraction part is \(\dfrac{1}{6}\).
Put the whole number part and the fraction part together: 1 and \(\dfrac{1}{6}\).
Check by adding: the answer plus the amount taken away must give the starting amount (shown here as decimals).
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the denominators as well (only the numerators are subtracted), one is a piece too big, one a piece too small, and one adds instead of subtracting.

keyPoints.note: A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

steps.explain: Method 2 (multiply): write 20 as \(\dfrac{20}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(3 \times  20 = 60\), denominator × denominator = \(5 \times  1 = 5\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{60}{5}\): the highest common factor of 60 and 5 is 5. Divide the top and the bottom by 5.
Both methods give 12 chocolate bars.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

steps.explain: Method 2 (multiply): write 20 as \(\dfrac{20}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(3 \times  20 = 60\), denominator × denominator = \(4 \times  1 = 4\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{60}{4}\): the highest common factor of 60 and 4 is 4. Divide the top and the bottom by 4.
Both methods give 15 counters.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

steps.explain: Method 2 (multiply): write 60 as \(\dfrac{60}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(3 \times  60 = 180\), denominator × denominator = \(4 \times  1 = 4\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{180}{4}\): the highest common factor of 180 and 4 is 4. Divide the top and the bottom by 4.
Both methods give 45 counters.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

steps.explain: Method 2 (multiply): write 56 as \(\dfrac{56}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(1 \times  56 = 56\), denominator × denominator = \(8 \times  1 = 8\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{56}{8}\): the highest common factor of 56 and 8 is 8. Divide the top and the bottom by 8.
Both methods give 7 counters.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.

steps.explain: Method 2 (multiply): write 56 as \(\dfrac{56}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(7 \times  56 = 392\), denominator × denominator = \(8 \times  1 = 8\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{392}{8}\): the highest common factor of 392 and 8 is 8. Divide the top and the bottom by 8.
Both methods give 49 counters.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.

questions.hint: Divide by the denominator (6), then multiply by the numerator (1).

steps.explain: '\(\dfrac{1}{6}\) of 48' means \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) × 48. Think of the 48 as 6 equal groups; the numerator 1 says how many of the groups we take.

questions.stem: Use counters to find the fraction of each collection. \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) of 100 counters
questions.hint: Divide by the denominator (5), then multiply by the numerator (1).

steps.explain: '\(\dfrac{1}{5}\) of 100' means \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) × 100. Think of the 100 as 5 equal groups; the numerator 1 says how many of the groups we take.
Method 1 (groups): divide 100 into 5 equal groups: \(100 \div  5 = 20\). One group is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) of 100.
Take 1 group: \(1 \times  20 = 20\).
Method 2 (multiply): write 100 as \(\dfrac{100}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(1 \times  100 = 100\), denominator × denominator = \(5 \times  1 = 5\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{100}{5}\): the highest common factor of 100 and 5 is 5. Divide the top and the bottom by 5.
Both methods give 20 counters.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

questions.stem: Calculate this. Draw a picture to help. \(\dfrac{2}{9}\) of 162
questions.hint: Divide by the denominator (9), then multiply by the numerator (2).

steps.explain: '\(\dfrac{2}{9}\) of 162' means \(\dfrac{2}{9}\) × 162. Think of the 162 as 9 equal groups; the numerator 2 says how many of the groups we take.
Method 1 (groups): divide 162 into 9 equal groups: \(162 \div  9 = 18\). One group is \(\dfrac{1}{9}\) of 162.
Take 2 groups: \(2 \times  18 = 36\).
Method 2 (multiply): write 162 as \(\dfrac{162}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(2 \times  162 = 324\), denominator × denominator = \(9 \times  1 = 9\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{324}{9}\): the highest common factor of 324 and 9 is 9. Divide the top and the bottom by 9.
Both methods give 36.
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

keyPoints.note: Read what the question asks, then choose a method.

questions.stem: There are 5 people in the O'Brien family: Mum, Dad and three children. Dad bought 15 potatoes for dinner. These were to be shared equally, but then Mum and one of the children went out to have dinner with a friend. How many of the potatoes should Mr O'Brien cook?
questions.hint: Find the fraction of the family at home, then take that fraction of 15.

steps.explain: There are 5 people in the O'Brien family: Mum, Dad and three children. Mum and one of the children went out, so 2 people are away.

steps.explain: The potatoes are shared equally, so the home group should get \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) of the 15 potatoes.
One fifth of 15 is \(15 \div  5 = 3\), so three fifths is \(3 \times  3 = 9\) potatoes.
Check: 2 people away should get \(2 \times  3 = 6\) potatoes, and \(9 + 6 = 15\). ✓
Why the other answers are wrong: 6 is the potatoes for the two people who are away; 3 is only one fifth of the potatoes; 15 is all the potatoes.

keyPoints.note: Work out what the question is counting, then use the fraction.

questions.stem: Do the multiplication and write the answer in simplest form: \(\dfrac{4}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{8}\)
questions.hint: Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together, then simplify.
questions.solution: Multiply numerators: \\\\(4 \times 3 = 12\\). Multiply denominators: \\\\(5 \times 8 = 40\\). The fraction is \\(\frac{12}{40}\\). Simplify by dividing top and bottom by \\\\(4\\) to get \\(\frac{3}{10}\\).

steps.explain: Multiply the numerators together.
Multiply the denominators together.
Simplify the resulting fraction by dividing by the highest common factor.

questions.stem: Emma saves \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) of her weekly allowance. Of the remainder, she spends \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) on snacks. What fraction of her total weekly allowance does she spend on snacks?
questions.hint: First, find the fraction that is the 'remainder'. Then multiply that remainder by the fraction she spends on snacks.
questions.solution: If she saves \\(\frac{3}{5}\\), the remainder is \\\\(1 - \frac{3}{5} = \frac{2}{5}\\). She spends \\(\frac{1}{3}\\) of this remainder on snacks. Multiply: \\(\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{5} = \frac{2}{15}\\). She spends \\(\frac{2}{15}\\) of her total allowance on snacks.

steps.explain: Calculate the remaining fraction of her allowance after saving.
Calculate what fraction of the total allowance is spent on snacks by multiplying the spent fraction by the remainder.
Multiply numerators and denominators.

questions.stem: The Tigers basketball team won \(16\) out of \(24\) matches. If \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) of these wins were by more than \(5\) points, what fraction of all the matches were won by more than \(5\) points?
questions.hint: First, find the total fraction of games won. Then multiply it by the fraction of wins that were by more than 5 points.
questions.solution: The fraction of matches won is \\(\frac{16}{24}\\), which simplifies to \\(\frac{2}{3}\\). We are told \\(\frac{3}{4}\\) of these wins were by more than \\\\(5\\) points. Multiply the two fractions: \\(\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2}\\). So, \\(\frac{1}{2}\\) of all matches were won by more than \\\\(5\\) points.

steps.explain: Find the fraction of total matches won and simplify it.
Multiply this fraction by the fraction of wins that were by >5 points.
Multiply and simplify.

questions.stem: Tina's brother eats half of a piece of cake that is half of the whole cake. What fraction of the whole cake is that? \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
questions.hint: Multiply the numerators, multiply the denominators, then simplify.

steps.explain: To multiply two fractions, multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together. ('of' means multiply.)
Multiply the numerators: \(1 \times  1 = 1\). Multiply the denominators: \(2 \times  2 = 4\).
Check with decimals (estimate): multiply the decimal values.
Why the other answers are wrong: adding the numerators and denominators is not multiplication; the others double or halve the answer or add the fractions instead.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.

questions.stem: To multiply two fractions, multiply the numerators and then multiply the denominators. Use this to calculate \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) of \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).
questions.hint: Multiply the numerators, multiply the denominators, then simplify.

steps.explain: To multiply two fractions, multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together. ('of' means multiply.)
Multiply the numerators: \(3 \times  2 = 6\). Multiply the denominators: \(4 \times  3 = 12\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{6}{12}\): the highest common factor of 6 and 12 is 6. Divide the top and the bottom by 6.
Check with decimals (estimate): multiply the decimal values.
Why the other answers are wrong: adding the numerators and denominators is not multiplication; the others double or halve the answer or add the fractions instead.

keyPoints.note: The numerator is the number of parts we are interested in.
The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.

questions.stem: Craig spent \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) of his money at the show. Of the money he spent, \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) was spent on showbags and the rest was spent on rides. Craig spent \(\$36\) on rides. How much money did he spend on showbags?
questions.hint: Rides are 3 of 4 equal parts of the money spent. Find one part.

steps.explain: Craig spent \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) of his money at the show. Of that spent money, \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) went on showbags and the rest on rides, so rides are the remaining \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) of the spent money.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 60" width="100%" height="auto" style="max-width:330px;display:block;margin:0 auto"><rect x="10.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#fcd34d" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/><rect x="80.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#fcd34d" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/><rect x="150.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#fcd34d" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/><rect x="220.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#a5b4fc" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/></svg>

steps.explain: Craig spent 36 dollars on rides, which is 3 of the 4 equal parts of the money he spent.
One part is 36 dollars shared into 3 equal parts, which is 12 dollars. That is the money spent on showbags (1 part).
The money he spent in total is 4 parts of 12 dollars, which is 48 dollars.
Why the other answers are wrong: 48 dollars is the total he spent; 36 dollars is the rides; 9 dollars divides by 4 instead of by 3.

keyPoints.note: Read what the question asks, then choose a method.

questions.stem: Craig spent \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) of his money at the show. Of the money he spent, \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) was spent on showbags and the rest was spent on rides. Craig spent \(\$36\) on rides. How much money did Craig begin with?
questions.hint: Find the money spent first, then remember that was half of what he started with.

steps.explain: Craig spent \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) of his money at the show. Of that spent money, \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) went on showbags and the rest on rides, so rides are the remaining \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) of the spent money.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 60" width="100%" height="auto" style="max-width:330px;display:block;margin:0 auto"><rect x="10.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#fcd34d" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/><rect x="80.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#fcd34d" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/><rect x="150.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#fcd34d" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/><rect x="220.0" y="10" width="70.0" height="40" fill="#a5b4fc" stroke="#2f3e9e" stroke-width="2.4"/></svg>

steps.explain: Craig spent 36 dollars on rides, which is 3 of the 4 equal parts of the money he spent.
One part is 36 dollars shared into 3 equal parts, which is 12 dollars. That is the money spent on showbags (1 part).
The money he spent in total is 4 parts of 12 dollars, which is 48 dollars.
This is half of the money he started with, so he began with double 48 dollars, which is 96 dollars.
Check: half of 96 dollars is 48 dollars; one quarter of 48 dollars is 12 dollars (showbags) and three quarters is 36 dollars (rides).

questions.stem: The fraction \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) represents which division, and what is its decimal value?
questions.hint: A fraction \(\dfrac{a}{b}\) represents \(a\div b\).

steps.explain: A fraction \(\dfrac{a}{b}\) means \(a\) divided by \(b\).
Evaluate the division.

questions.stem: 7 children share a box of 29 mangoes equally. How many mangoes does each child get?
questions.hint: Write the division as a fraction (the number being divided on top), then simplify or write a mixed number.

steps.explain: Dividing a whole number by a whole number can give a fraction: 29 ÷ 7 means 29 shared equally into 7 parts, which is the fraction \(\dfrac{29}{7}\).
If the answer is bigger than 1, write it as a mixed number: how many lots of 7 are in 29? \(7 \times  4 = 28\), and \(29 - 28 = 1\) is left over.
Check: multiply the answer by the number you divided by: you must get the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one has the numbers the wrong way round, one is a piece too big, one is a piece too small, and one has not been simplified/halved correctly.

keyPoints.note: Work out what the question is counting, then use the fraction.

questions.stem: Suppose 4 children share 3 giant lolly snakes equally. How much of a snake does each child receive?
questions.hint: Write the division as a fraction (the number being divided on top), then simplify or write a mixed number.

steps.explain: Dividing a whole number by a whole number can give a fraction: 3 ÷ 4 means 3 shared equally into 4 parts, which is the fraction \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).
If the answer is bigger than 1, write it as a mixed number: how many lots of 4 are in 3? \(4 \times  0 = 0\), and \(3 - 0 = 3\) is left over.
There are no whole lots of 4 in 3, so the answer is just the fraction \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).
Check: multiply the answer by the number you divided by: you must get the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one has the numbers the wrong way round, one is a piece too big, one is a piece too small, and one has not been simplified/halved correctly.

keyPoints.note: Read what the question asks, then choose a method.

questions.stem: Suppose 4 children share 5 jam tarts equally. How much does each child receive?
questions.hint: Write the division as a fraction (the number being divided on top), then simplify or write a mixed number.

steps.explain: Dividing a whole number by a whole number can give a fraction: 5 ÷ 4 means 5 shared equally into 4 parts, which is the fraction \(\dfrac{5}{4}\).
If the answer is bigger than 1, write it as a mixed number: how many lots of 4 are in 5? \(4 \times  1 = 4\), and \(5 - 4 = 1\) is left over.
So \(\dfrac{5}{4}\) = 1 and \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) left over: 5 ÷ 4 = \(1\dfrac{1}{4}\).
Check: multiply the answer by the number you divided by: you must get the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one has the numbers the wrong way round, one is a piece too big, one is a piece too small, and one has not been simplified/halved correctly.

keyPoints.note: Read what the question asks, then choose a method.

steps.explain: Dividing a whole number by a whole number can give a fraction: 12 ÷ 13 means 12 shared equally into 13 parts, which is the fraction \(\dfrac{12}{13}\).
If the answer is bigger than 1, write it as a mixed number: how many lots of 13 are in 12? \(13 \times  0 = 0\), and \(12 - 0 = 12\) is left over.
There are no whole lots of 13 in 12, so the answer is just the fraction \(\dfrac{12}{13}\).
Check: multiply the answer by the number you divided by: you must get the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one has the numbers the wrong way round, one is a piece too big, one is a piece too small, and one has not been simplified/halved correctly.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Divide the top and bottom by their biggest common factor.
A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

questions.stem: Ginny takes 3 identical cakes and cuts each one into 12 equal pieces. She has exactly the right number of pieces to give everyone at her party \(\dfrac{1}{12}\) of a cake. How many people are at her party? Calculate 3 ÷ \(\dfrac{1}{12}\).
questions.hint: Invert the second fraction and multiply; then simplify.

steps.explain: To divide by a fraction, INVERT the fraction (turn it upside down) and MULTIPLY. Dividing asks 'how many lots of the second amount fit into the first?'.
Write the whole number 3 as a fraction: 3=\(\dfrac{3}{1}\).
Invert the second fraction: \(\dfrac{1}{12}\) becomes \(\dfrac{12}{1}\). Change the ÷ sign to ×.
Multiply the numerators: \(3 \times  12 = 36\). Multiply the denominators: \(1 \times  1 = 1\).
Check by multiplying back: answer × the number we divided by must give the first number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one MULTIPLIES by the fraction without inverting it, one inverts the wrong fraction, and the others are one out.

keyPoints.note: Work out what the question is counting, then use the fraction.

questions.hint: How many pieces of that size fit? Invert the fraction and multiply (whole number × denominator ÷ numerator).

steps.explain: 'How many \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) in 25?' is the division 25 ÷ \(\dfrac{1}{4}\).
Each whole has 4 pieces of size \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). So 25 wholes have \(25 \times  4 = 100\) pieces of size \(\dfrac{1}{4}\).
We need groups of 1 pieces (each group is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\)). Divide the pieces into groups of 1: \(100 \div  1 = 100\).
Using the rule: invert \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) and multiply: 25 × \(\dfrac{4}{1}\) = \(\dfrac{100}{1}\) = 100.
Check: multiply back.
Why the other answers are wrong: one MULTIPLIES by the fraction (finding a fraction OF the number), one is one out, and one divides by the denominator only.

keyPoints.note: Work out what the question is counting, then use the fraction.

steps.explain: \(\dfrac{7}{5}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(7 \div  5 = 1\) remainder 2.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.
Proper fraction: numerator is smaller than the denominator.

questions.hint: Same denominator: add the numerators and keep the denominator; then simplify.

questions.stem: Draw a number line to calculate this addition. \(\dfrac{5}{18}\) + \(\dfrac{11}{18}\)
questions.hint: Same denominator: add the numerators and keep the denominator; then simplify.

steps.explain: The fractions have the SAME denominator 18, so we are adding 18ths: the size of each piece stays the same and we just count pieces.
Add the numerators and keep the denominator 18: \(5 + 11 = 16\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{16}{18}\): the highest common factor of 16 and 18 is 2, so divide the top and the bottom by 2.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.

questions.stem: Add these fractions. \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) + \(\dfrac{3}{4}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (3, 4), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 3, 4.
List multiples: multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12 ; multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. The lowest common multiple is 12.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) to 12ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 4 (because \(3 \times  4 = 12\)).

questions.stem: Add these fractions. \(\dfrac{12}{15}\) + \(\dfrac{5}{20}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (15, 20), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 15, 20.
List multiples: multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60 ; multiples of 20: 20, 40, 60. The lowest common multiple is 60.
Change \(\dfrac{12}{15}\) to 60ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 4 (because \(15 \times  4 = 60\)).
Change \(\dfrac{5}{20}\) to 60ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(20 \times  3 = 60\)).
Now every fraction has denominator 60. Add the numerators: \(48 + 15 = 63\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{63}{60}\): the highest common factor of 63 and 60 is 3, so divide the top and the bottom by 3.
\(\dfrac{21}{20}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(21 \div  20 = 1\) remainder 1.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{12}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{8}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (3, 12, 8), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 3, 8, 12.
List multiples: multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 ; multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. The lowest common multiple is 24.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) to 24ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 8 (because \(3 \times  8 = 24\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 20. Add the numerators: \(4 + 6 + 7 + 14 = 31\).
\(\dfrac{31}{20}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(31 \div  20 = 1\) remainder 11.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) + \(\dfrac{5}{6}\) + \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) + \(\dfrac{5}{12}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (3, 6, 9, 12), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 3, 6, 9, 12.
List multiples: multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 ; multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 ; multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36 ; multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. The lowest common multiple is 36.
Change \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) to 36ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 12 (because \(3 \times  12 = 36\)).
Change \(\dfrac{5}{6}\) to 36ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 6 (because \(6 \times  6 = 36\)).
Change \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) to 36ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 4 (because \(9 \times  4 = 36\)).
Change \(\dfrac{5}{12}\) to 36ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(12 \times  3 = 36\)).
Now every fraction has denominator 36. Add the numerators: \(24 + 30 + 16 + 15 = 85\).
\(\dfrac{85}{36}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(85 \div  36 = 2\) remainder 13.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (16, 8, 4, 16), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4, 8, 16.
List multiples: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 ; multiples of 16: 16, 32, 48. The lowest common multiple is 16.
Change \(\dfrac{3}{16}\) to 16ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 1 (because \(16 \times  1 = 16\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 16. Add the numerators: \(3 + 6 + 12 + 5 = 26\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{26}{16}\): the highest common factor of 26 and 16 is 2, so divide the top and the bottom by 2.
\(\dfrac{13}{8}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(13 \div  8 = 1\) remainder 5.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 7: Fraction arithmetic

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{7}{10}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{15}\) + \(\dfrac{11}{30}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{5}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (10, 15, 30, 5), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 5, 10, 15, 30.
List multiples: multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 ; multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30 ; multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45 ; multiples of 30: 30, 60, 90. The lowest common multiple is 30.
Change \(\dfrac{7}{10}\) to 30ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 3 (because \(10 \times  3 = 30\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 30. Add the numerators: \(21 + 2 + 11 + 6 = 40\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{40}{30}\): the highest common factor of 40 and 30 is 10, so divide the top and the bottom by 10.
\(\dfrac{4}{3}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(4 \div  3 = 1\) remainder 1.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 7: Fraction arithmetic

questions.stem: Convert the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add them. \(\dfrac{1}{14}\) + \(\dfrac{6}{7}\) + \(\dfrac{4}{7}\) + \(\dfrac{9}{14}\) + \(\dfrac{1}{7}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (14, 7, 7, 14, 7), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 7, 14.
List multiples: multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21 ; multiples of 14: 14, 28, 42. The lowest common multiple is 14.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{14}\) to 14ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 1 (because \(14 \times  1 = 14\)).

steps.explain: Now every fraction has denominator 14. Add the numerators: \(1 + 12 + 8 + 9 + 2 = 32\).
Simplify \(\dfrac{32}{14}\): the highest common factor of 32 and 14 is 2, so divide the top and the bottom by 2.
\(\dfrac{16}{7}\) is an improper fraction. Write it as a mixed number: \(16 \div  7 = 2\) remainder 2.
Check with a quick estimate: change each fraction to a decimal and add (or use the number line); the total should agree.
Why the other answers are wrong: one adds the denominators as well (only the numerators are added when the denominators match), one is one piece too big and one is one piece too small.

keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

questions.stem: At the end of their holiday, the Russell family drove back home from Fingal Bay to Brunswick. On the first day, Mrs Russell drove \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of the distance. On the second day, Mr Russell drove \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) of the distance and Mrs Russell drove \(\dfrac{5}{16}\) of the distance. How much of the distance home had the Russells driven in those two days?
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same (lowest common multiple), add the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: The denominators are different (4, 8, 16), so we cannot add the pieces yet. Find a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 4, 8, 16.
List multiples: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16 ; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 ; multiples of 16: 16, 32, 48. The lowest common multiple is 16.
Change \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) to 16ths: multiply the top and the bottom by 4 (because \(4 \times  4 = 16\)).

questions.stem: Work out this subtraction. \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) − \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are the same (3), so we take away 1 pieces from 2 pieces. Each piece is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\); the crossed-out pieces are taken away.

questions.stem: Work out this subtraction. \(\dfrac{7}{10}\) − \(\dfrac{2}{5}\)
questions.hint: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, then simplify.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away: start with the first amount and take the second away.
The denominators are different (10 and 5). Change both fractions to a common denominator: the lowest common multiple of 10 and 5 is 10.
Change \(\dfrac{7}{10}\) to 10ths: multiply top and bottom by 1. (It already has this denominator.)

steps.explain: As a fraction of the potting mix: kilograms left over the total kilograms.
Simplify: the highest common factor of 6 and 15 is 3. Divide the top and the bottom by 3.
Check: used fraction is \(\dfrac{9}{15}\) = \(\dfrac{3}{5}\), and \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) + \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) = 1 whole. ✓

steps.explain: Method 1 (groups): divide 9 into 5 equal groups: \(9 \div  5 = 1.8\). One group is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) of 9.
Take 2 groups: \(2 \times  1.8 = 3.6\).
Method 2 (multiply): write 9 as \(\dfrac{9}{1}\) and multiply: numerator × numerator = \(2 \times  9 = 18\), denominator × denominator = \(5 \times  1 = 5\).
\(\dfrac{18}{5}\) is an improper fraction (numerator bigger than denominator). Divide: \(18 \div  5 = 3\) remainder 3, so it is 3 and \(\dfrac{3}{5}\).
Both methods give \(3\dfrac{3}{5}\).
Why the other answers are wrong: one finds the remaining part (the groups NOT taken), one adds instead of multiplying, one is one out, and one divides by the numerator instead of the denominator.

questions.stem: Find the value of this division. Write your answer as a fraction or mixed number in its simplest form. 3 ÷ 5
questions.hint: Write the division as a fraction (the number being divided on top), then simplify or write a mixed number.

steps.explain: Dividing a whole number by a whole number can give a fraction: 3 ÷ 5 means 3 shared equally into 5 parts, which is the fraction \(\dfrac{3}{5}\).
If the answer is bigger than 1, write it as a mixed number: how many lots of 5 are in 3? \(5 \times  0 = 0\), and \(3 - 0 = 3\) is left over.
There are no whole lots of 5 in 3, so the answer is just the fraction \(\dfrac{3}{5}\).
Check: multiply the answer by the number you divided by: you must get the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one has the numbers the wrong way round, one is a piece too big, one is a piece too small, and one has not been simplified/halved correctly.

keyPoints.note: A fraction = shaded (or chosen) parts ÷ total equal parts.
Divide the top and bottom by their biggest common factor.
A mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction.

questions.stem: Calculate, and simplify where you can. 21 ÷ \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
questions.hint: Invert the second fraction and multiply; then simplify.

steps.explain: To divide by a fraction, INVERT the fraction (turn it upside down) and MULTIPLY. Dividing asks 'how many lots of the second amount fit into the first?'.
Write the whole number 21 as a fraction: 21=\(\dfrac{21}{1}\).
Invert the second fraction: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) becomes \(\dfrac{3}{1}\). Change the ÷ sign to ×.
Multiply the numerators: \(21 \times  3 = 63\). Multiply the denominators: \(1 \times  1 = 1\).
Check by multiplying back: answer × the number we divided by must give the first number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one MULTIPLIES by the fraction without inverting it, one inverts the wrong fraction, and the others are one out.
